opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a great question, and honestly one I think about a lot, because it goes to the heart of where all this infrastructure we're building is ultimately going to land.

When I say "AI-only" or "AI-native" companies, I mean businesses designed from day one around the assumption that intelligence is cheap, abundant, and available on demand. That's very different from an established company bolting a chatbot onto an existing workflow. The AI-native company doesn't have legacy processes to protect. It asks, "If I could have a capable reasoning engine handle most of this work, what would the business look like?" The answers are often radically leaner organizations: a handful of people orchestrating fleets of agents doing what used to take hundreds.

The first areas to be reshaped will be the ones where the work is already digital and information-heavy. Think customer support, software development, legal research and document review, financial analysis, insurance claims, marketing content. The inputs and outputs there are already text, code, or structured data, so the friction is low. You're already seeing startups with very small teams generating revenue that would historically have needed a much larger headcount.

The second wave is more interesting to me, and it's where things get physical: healthcare, logistics, manufacturing, energy. AI-native companies there will pair models with sensors, robotics, and real-world operations. That takes longer because you're dealing with regulation, safety, and atoms instead of bits, but the economic prize is much larger.

There's an important caveat, though, and it comes from where I sit on the infrastructure side. None of this happens at scale unless the cost of running these models, the cost of inference, comes down dramatically. Training gets the headlines, but an AI-native company's cost of goods sold is essentially inference. Every customer interaction, every agent step, every reasoning chain consumes compute. If a token is too expensive or too slow, the business model breaks. A company that wants to run thousands of agents continuously needs inference that's fast, power-efficient, and economical. So I see the hardware and systems layer as the gating factor that determines how quickly these AI-native businesses can actually reshape the economy.

And as inference gets cheaper, you get a Jevons paradox effect: demand doesn't just grow, it explodes. Use cases that made no economic sense at a dollar per thousand queries suddenly make perfect sense at a fraction of a cent. That's when you'll see AI-native companies show up in every corner of the economy, including places nobody is thinking about today.

So I'm very optimistic. I think we'll look back on this period the way we look at the early internet, when people were building websites but hadn't yet imagined Uber or Airbnb. The truly transformative AI-native companies probably haven't been founded yet, and a big part of what will enable them is getting the economics of inference right.

r001.rationale: The response names digital, information-heavy fields as early areas for change, but does not say their offerings can be fully automated.

r002.rationale: It describes lean AI-native companies but does not recommend that incumbent companies redeploy workers to tasks AI handles poorly.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss human involvement in selling or the role of buyers’ emotions.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think we're at a really interesting moment, because for the first time you can imagine a company where AI isn't a feature bolted onto an existing business, it's the business. And when you start from that premise, a lot of assumptions about how companies are built just fall away.

Take the traditional software company. You hire a lot of engineers, you build a product, you hire a sales force, you hire support. Headcount scales roughly with revenue. An AI-only company flips that. You might have a very small team, and the leverage comes from models and compute rather than people. That changes the cost structure, it changes how fast you can move, and it changes what kinds of markets are even worth going after. Niches that were too small to justify a two hundred person company suddenly make sense for a team of ten.

Where I think this gets most interesting is in the parts of the economy that have historically been services businesses. Legal, accounting, customer support, back-office operations, a lot of healthcare administration. These are enormous markets, but they've resisted software because the work was too messy, too unstructured, too dependent on judgment. Now you can build a company that delivers the outcome of that service, not just a tool to help a human do it. That's a very different value proposition, and it's where I expect to see a lot of the new entrants.

The other side of it, which I spend a lot of my time thinking about, is that all of this runs on infrastructure. If your company is AI-only, then compute is your cost of goods sold. The economics of inference, how much it costs to serve a query, how much latency you can tolerate, where that compute physically lives, those become first-order business questions rather than something the IT department handles. We've had a decade of cloud infrastructure optimized for training and for the hyperscalers. I think the next decade is about inference infrastructure that's efficient enough to make these AI-native business models actually profitable at scale, including at the edge where a lot of real-world work happens.

So my short answer is that the reshaping happens in two layers. At the top, you get a wave of lean companies going after service-heavy industries that software never cracked. Underneath, you get a rebuild of the compute stack to make those companies viable. And I think the second part is what people underestimate, because the models get the headlines, but the margins get decided in silicon.

r001.rationale: The candidate names service-heavy industries as likely targets for AI-native entrants, but does not say the offerings can be fully automated or that these are the earliest targets.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not recommend redeploying incumbent workers to tasks AI performs poorly.

r003.rationale: The candidate does not discuss human involvement in selling or the emotional appeal to human buyers.

astra-6.text:
I think the potential is enormous, but it will play out differently across industries. In software, you can imagine a very small team using AI to build a product, support customers, and run much of the business. That changes the economics of starting a company and how quickly it can scale.

As you move into healthcare, manufacturing, or transportation, there’s a physical component, there’s accountability, and there are consequences when something goes wrong. AI can do a lot of the work, but an entirely AI-operated company is a much bigger leap.

So I’d distinguish between AI-only companies and companies built around AI from day one. The second category could reshape a huge part of the economy well before we get to the first. If a small team can deliver something that previously required hundreds of people, that creates opportunities for new businesses and puts pressure on incumbents to rethink how they operate. The question becomes: where does human judgment add the most value, and how do you organize the company around that?

r001.rationale: The response says software is more suited to small AI-enabled teams and that fully AI-operated companies are a bigger leap elsewhere, but it does not identify businesses with fully automatable offerings as the earliest targets.

r002.rationale: It asks where human judgment adds value and says incumbents may need to rethink how they operate, but does not recommend redeploying incumbent workers to tasks AI performs poorly.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss selling products or appealing to buyers’ emotions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the opportunity is enormous, particularly in areas where the work is largely digital. You can imagine companies where AI handles much of the software development, customer support, marketing, and back-office operations, with a small number of people setting direction and taking responsibility for the outcomes. That changes the economics of starting and scaling a business.

But I think it will happen task by task, rather than entire industries suddenly becoming autonomous. Handling a routine customer inquiry is very different from making a consequential financial or medical decision. The question is how reliably these systems can operate, how you verify their work, and when they need to bring a human in.

If we get that right, you could see very small companies serving markets that previously weren’t economical to serve. That’s potentially as significant as making existing businesses more efficient: it opens up room for entirely new businesses.

r001.rationale: The response discusses AI handling digital work and says adoption will happen task by task, but it does not identify fully automatable offerings as the earliest targets for AI-only competitors.

r002.rationale: It mentions people setting direction and stepping in when systems need human involvement, but does not recommend that incumbent companies redeploy workers to tasks AI performs poorly.

r003.rationale: The response does not connect human involvement in selling to appealing to buyers’ emotions.
